overall_structure.value: After solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching the Mn-35 steel (Fe34.23Mn11.10Al1.00C) consists of a single austenite (FCC) phase — no ferrite — with a coarse austenite grain size of about 33 μm, a twin boundary fraction of about 60% and uniformly distributed nano-scale κ-carbides of about 2 nm.

source.reason: For the 35%Mn sample only a single austenite phase is present with average grain size about 33 μm and twin boundary fraction about 60%; Table 3 lists D_FCC-G/T 33 ± 1.6 μm, f_Tw 59.6%, D_κ-carbides 2.0 ± 1.1 nm; the κ-carbide size of ~2 nm is stated for 35%Mn.

phase_evolution.value: No ferrite present at 35%Mn; only a single austenite phase after solution treatment. κ-carbide precipitation originates from spinodal decomposition and ordering of C and Al in the austenite; κ-carbide size decreases with increasing Mn content (5 nm at 25%Mn to 2 nm at 35%Mn).

interface_notes.value: The κ-carbides assume a coherent interface with the austenite matrix as evidenced by SAED observations; strengthening therefore follows a particle shear model rather than Orowan.

Nominal/measured chemical composition of the Mn-35 steel (Table 1): C 1.00, Mn 34.23, Al 11.10, Fe Bal., density 6.53 g/cm3.
The Mn-35 steel shows the largest austenite grain size (~33 μm) and the softest grade (YS ~401 MPa) among the investigated compositions.
The κ-carbide size decreases with increasing Mn content: 5 nm at 25%Mn to 2 nm at 35%Mn; the 35%Mn sample shows the finest and most sparsely resolved κ-carbide particles of the Mn series.

Except for the 0.6%C and 30%Mn steels, the work hardening rate vs true strain of the other steels (including 35%Mn) shows a typical behaviour: a rapid decline followed by a slow rise and then another decline (the 0.6%C and 30%Mn steels show a monotonic decrease).
